title: Progressive Traffic Controller + Orchestrator Fallback Policy for Hosted API Upgrades
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Objective: Harden the Hosted API deployment pipeline by implementing a progressive traffic controller combined with an orchestrator-level fallback policy. This ticket designs and implements an automated controller that performs SLO-driven progressive rollouts across regions and model/version channels, and automatically reroutes traffic to healthy variants (green) or older LTS channels when degradation is detected.

Scope and components to deliver:
- Traffic controller service: accepts deployment intents (version X in region R) and executes weight-adjustment plans with rate limits, cooldowns and maximum step sizes.
- SLO-based gates: gating decisions use latency (p50/p95/p99), error rate (5xx and malformed responses), quality regressions (synthetic prompt score delta) and token cost deltas.
- Regional awareness: controller must understand region capacity, cross-region latency penalties, and infra reservation constraints.
- Fallback policy engine: when a gate trips, controller automatically shifts traffic to a fallback target (previous version, LTS channel, or dedicated capacity pool) with configurable drain windows.
- KV-cache warmers and prefix cache hints: before shifting large traffic to a new variant, pre-warm caches for top-traffic prefixes to reduce cold-start latency spikes.
- Observability & runbooks: dashboards for rollout progress, per-version token-level cost and quality deltas, and an automated incident runbook triggered when a fallback executes.
- Safety primitives: global kill-switch, per-customer holdbacks (for enterprise customers), manual approval hooks, and audit logs for rollforward/rollback decisions.

Design decisions & trade-offs considered:
- Strict SLO thresholds vs. adaptive baselines: we will use adaptive baselines for p95/p99 (rolling-window median + multiplier) to avoid noisy rollbacks caused by diurnal shifts, but keep absolute caps for error-rate spikes.
- Step size and cadence: conservative default of 5% weight steps every 5 minutes with a configurable faster profile for low-risk stateless models.
- Automatic rollback vs. partial fallback: prefer partial fallback (shift only failing region or cohort) over global rollback to minimize blast radius. Full rollback reserved for catastrophic regressions.
- Cache warmers increase platform complexity but materially reduce latency regressions during traffic shifts; therefore they are required for models with >20% cold-cache latency delta.

Implementation notes and artifacts:
- Controller will be implemented as a Kubernetes-native controller in the orchestrator service repo. See design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RE/Progressive+Traffic+Controller (draft).
- Has a feature flag (flagservice:progressive_traffic_controller) and per-tenant allowlist for early opt-in.
- GitHub PR template links: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/452 (WIP).
- Synthetic workload harness: workload definitions stored in infra-tests/synthetic-rollout-harness.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
1) Controller can schedule a progressive rollout for a new hosted-api version across at least 3 regions with >95% successful weight updates and accurate state reconciliation after restarts.
2) SLO gates detect degradations within the configured window and trigger fallback within 10 minutes, shifting >90% of affected traffic to fallback targets without manual intervention.
3) Cache warming reduces p95 latency spike during large (>20%) weight shifts by at least 30% in synthetic tests.
4) Dashboards show per-step metrics, and every controller decision is logged to audit stream and surfaced in Console (rollout timeline).
5) Runbook exercises completed in staging with SRE and oncall; simulated rollback and fallback drills recorded.

Rolling plan (execution steps):
- Week 1: Finalize design, runbook and safety knobs; PR for controller skeleton.
- Week 2: Implement weight-adjustment engine and reconcile loop; add basic gates (error-rate + p95).
- Week 3: Implement regional fallback and cache-warming hooks; add observability metrics and dashboards.
- Week 4: Run synthetic harness, iterate thresholds, add per-tenant holdbacks and enterprise allowlists.
- Week 5: Staging drills and runbook review; gradual opt-in on staging then internal canary orgs.
- Week 6: Limited public rollout for low-risk models, runtime-1.22+ only, monitor for 48 hours, then expand.

Rollout knobs to expose in Console/APIs:
- max_step_percent (default 5), cooldown_seconds (default 300), gate_window_seconds (default 600), fallback_target (previous-version | lts-channel | dedicated-pool), prewarm_prefix_count (default 200), emergency_kill_switch (boolean), per_customer_holdback (boolean).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Inaccurate SLO signals cause oscillation. Mitigation: use combined signals (latency + errors + quality) and require multiple consecutive breached windows before action.
- Risk: Fallback target saturated. Mitigation: reserve capacity pool for rollbacks and pre-check fallback headroom before shifting.
- Risk: Cache-warming increases tail traffic and cost. Mitigation: throttle warmers and use sampling heuristics for prefix selection.

Notes: This ticket expands on prior deployment work (ENG-4271, ENG-9031, ENG-16457) but introduces automatic fallback to LTS channels, cache-warming integration, and per-tenant holdbacks to reduce enterprise risk.
acceptance_criteria: Progressive rollout across 3 regions completes with state reconciliation after controller restarts
SLO gate triggers fallback and shifts affected traffic within 10 minutes in staging synthetic tests
Cache warming demonstrably reduces p95 latency spikes by >=30% during large weight shifts
All controller actions are auditable and surfaced in Console rollout timeline
Runbook exercises completed and documented with SRE sign-off
